clue.text: Bottle of wine, old man?

definitions.meaning: a very large wine bottle holding eight standard bottles
the biblical patriarch said to have lived 969 years, a byword for great age

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a big bottle of wine is meant for an elderly gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant champagne bottle is named after the longest-lived patriarch of Genesis, whose name stands for any very aged person.

clue.text: English still showing stiff upper lip?

parts.note: still means not moving

explanation.surface: The English are still noted for keeping a stiff upper lip.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'stiff upper lip' is British restraint, not showing one's feelings; 'still' looks like an adverb meaning 'even now'.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping a stiff upper lip means hiding one's feelings, appearing unmoved.

clue.text: Join fellow director

parts.note: to hitch is to join or fasten
cock is old British slang for a man or chap, as in 'old cock'

explanation.surface: An invitation to team up with another film-maker.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Hitchcock was the famous British-born film director of thrillers such as Psycho.

clue.text: Engineers in military group put things straight

indicators.note: the engineers are placed inside the military group

parts.note: a squad is a small group of soldiers
RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps

explanation.surface: Army engineers within a unit tidy things up.
explanation.definitionFit: To square things is to settle or resolve them, so squared means put right.

clue.text: Needing a lot of staff, like the Commons now?

definitions.meaning: requiring many workers, as a heavy industry does
the House of Commons with a big Labour Party majority, packed with Labour members

explanation.surface: A remark that Parliament's lower house currently needs many employees.
explanation.walkthrough: The Commons is Britain's elected chamber and Labour a major party, so a House packed with Labour MPs is read as 'Labour-intensive'.
explanation.definitionFit: An industry demanding much manual work is so described; the pun reads it as dense with Labour MPs.

clue.text: High and mighty, showing extremes of humility about nothing

indicators.note: the outer letters go around the word for nothing
the first and last letters of the word humility

parts.note: aught (also ought) is an old word for nothing, zero

explanation.surface: An arrogant person is the very opposite of humble about nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High and mighty' is one phrase meaning arrogant; 'showing' links it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A haughty person is arrogant and proud, which is what 'high and mighty' describes.

clue.text: Talking bird

definitions.meaning: conversing in an easy, informal way
a small songbird such as the stonechat or whinchat

explanation.definitionFit: Informal conversation is one sense; the other is the name of a small songbird family.

clue.text: Equipment in gym for runner

definitions.meaning: the vaulting apparatus used in gymnastics

explanation.definitionFit: Gymnasts vault over a padded apparatus with this name, and a racing animal is a runner at the track.

clue.text: Receptacle in our opinion's right in the middle

indicators.note: the letter for right goes into the centre of the phrase

parts.note: 'to us' means in our opinion, as in 'it seems to us'

explanation.surface: We think a container is properly placed at the centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Receptacle' is the botanical sense: the end of a flower stalk that carries the flower's parts.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany the torus is another name for the thickened stalk end bearing the petals.

clue.text: General nobody looked up to

parts.note: reads as an unpopular army officer, but means a famously tiny showman billed with a military title, whom nobody had to raise their eyes to see

explanation.surface: A disliked army commander whom no soldier respected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looked up to' suggests respect; literally it is about height. General Tom Thumb was the stage name of Charles Stratton, the tiny star of P. T. Barnum's shows.
explanation.definitionFit: The diminutive circus performer bore the honorary rank of General, and being so small, no one had to raise their gaze to see him.

clue.text: Moneydealer's safe in old city

indicators.note: one word sits inside another, as the safe thing is placed in the old city

parts.note: Ur is the ancient Sumerian city in Mesopotamia
safe means sure, certain

explanation.surface: A financier's strongbox is kept in some ancient town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'safe' looks like a strongbox noun but is the adjective meaning sure; the 's is 'is' linking definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A usurer lends money at interest, often extortionate, so is a dealer in money.

clue.text: More pay for working, we hear

indicators.note: says the word for paying someone to work is what we take in by ear, standing for a different spelling

parts.note: to hire someone is to pay them for their work

explanation.surface: Workers want a bigger wage for doing their job, so the rumour goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More pay' reads as one phrase, a rise; but 'More' alone is the definition and 'pay for working' gives HIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Higher can mean greater in amount, as in higher prices, so it stands for more.

clue.text: Girl Guide?

parts.note: reads as a member of the youth movement, but means a female who guides people to their seats

explanation.surface: A question about a member of the Girl Guides youth movement.
explanation.walkthrough: The Girl Guides are the British equivalent of Girl Scouts; here the words are taken literally, a woman who shows people the way.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who shows theatregoers or wedding guests to their places is literally a female guide.

clue.text: Aren't families in ship the best quality of people?

indicators.note: the two words are placed inside the abbreviation for ship

parts.note: SS stands for steamship
ain't is a colloquial form of aren't
lines are lineages or families

explanation.surface: A question whether the families on board aren't the finest sort of people.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: saints are the best of people, so their quality is saintliness.
explanation.definitionFit: Holiness is the characteristic of saints, people thought of as the very best.

clue.text: Fascinated by ignition, oddly

indicators.note: take the odd-numbered letters, first, third, fifth and seventh, of the word ignition

explanation.surface: Someone is gripped by how an engine starts.
explanation.definitionFit: Being keen on or enthusiastic about something is informally being 'into' it.

clue.text: Female cyclist with hike partly showing line of bloomers?

parts.note: Daisy rides the 'bicycle made for two' in the old music-hall song Daisy Bell
the chain is one part of a bicycle

explanation.surface: A woman on a bicycle reveals a row of baggy knickers.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloomers are old-fashioned loose knickers, named after the cycling-era reformer Amelia Bloomer; here they are flowers, things that bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: Children thread small flowers together stem to stem to make a garland, a string of blossoms.

clue.text: It's phoney, but contrived to be fascinating

definitions.note: a verb phrase, matching the verb in the answer

indicators.note: something contrived is artificially made up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something is fake, yet designed to captivate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'phoney' and 'contrived' both suggest fakery in the surface; only 'contrived' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To mesmerise or entrance someone is to captivate them completely.

clue.text: Find oneself tied up — hence irate expression

definitions.meaning: literally, to become tangled into a knot
a rude British dismissal, roughly 'go away!'

explanation.surface: Someone tangled in rope, and angry about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get knotted!' is a mildly rude British retort, like 'get lost!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally becoming knotted, and also a well-known exasperated British brush-off.

clue.text: Number resembling religious people, according to Marx

definitions.text: Number resembling religious people, according to Marx

parts.words: Number resembling religious people, according to Marx
parts.note: 'Number' means one made numb; Marx called religion the opium of the people, so believers are drugged

explanation.surface: A count of how many people Marx thought were religious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is not a figure but 'more numb'. Karl Marx wrote that religion is 'the opium of the people'.
explanation.definitionFit: Drugged with a narcotic, a person is dulled, as Marx thought faith dulled the masses.

clue.text: Plans town in England announced

indicators.note: spoken out, so the town's name stands for a word spelt differently

parts.note: Devizes is a market town in Wiltshire, England

explanation.surface: Proposals for an English town are made public.
explanation.walkthrough: Devizes is a market town in Wiltshire.
explanation.definitionFit: To devise is to plan or invent, so devises means plans as a verb.

clue.text: Way in which some butter gets hard

parts.note: a pat is a small flat portion of butter
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A remark about how a knob of butter goes solid.
explanation.definitionFit: A path is a track or route, a way from one place to another.

clue.text: 'e's associated with nation set free

parts.note: the dropped-aitch form of 'he's', giving its written letters E and S

indicators.note: the letters of the word nation are let loose and rearranged

explanation.surface: A cockney speaker says a man belongs to a country that won its liberty.
explanation.walkthrough: As a whole, the clue describes the man: he is linked to a nation set free, as Estonia regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Baltic republic that won back its independence in 1991 is a man tied to a liberated country.

clue.text: Some strategy Ptolemy needed for this?

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A question about what kind of plan the Ptolemaic ruler required.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ptolemies were the Greek dynasty that ruled this country until Cleopatra, so 'this' is the land a Ptolemy needed a strategy for.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ptolemaic kings ruled the Nile kingdom, so it is the land their strategy served.

clue.text: Drunk's too close for comfort

explanation.surface: Someone tipsy is standing uncomfortably near.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for inebriated, and also describing something fitting closely or narrow.

clue.text: Sounds like bottle pub provided for musician

indicators.note: says the two words that follow are spoken, giving a different spelling

parts.note: a vial is a small bottle and an inn is a pub, said together

explanation.surface: A drinks bottle supplied by a pub for a performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vial inn' said quickly sounds like the instrument; the instrument stands for its player, as in 'first violin'.
explanation.definitionFit: Orchestral players are named by instrument, so a violin can mean a violinist.

clue.text: Food you mostly swallow right into belly

indicators.note: most of the word you is kept, its final letter dropped
one letter is put inside the belly word

parts.note: gut is a word for the belly

explanation.surface: Advice to swallow something directly into the stomach.
explanation.definitionFit: A fermented milk product eaten as a snack or dessert is a food.

clue.text: Brilliant spin engineered dire collapse

indicators.note: something engineered is reconstructed, so spin is rearranged
the word dire falls apart and its letters reform

explanation.surface: A clever piece of PR spin brought about a terrible downfall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engineered' makes INSP from SPIN and 'collapse' makes IRED from DIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspired work is exceptionally clever or creative, as if driven by genius.

clue.text: Most of the members get no cover in this combination of unions

definitions.text: Most of the members get no cover in this

indicators.note: two of the abbreviation are joined, since the clue speaks of unions in the plural

parts.note: TU is the abbreviation for trade union

explanation.surface: In this alliance of trade unions, most members miss out on insurance.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'members' are limbs: a ballet dancer's short skirt leaves most of the legs uncovered.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballerina's short stiff skirt leaves the legs, most of the body's limbs, bare.

clue.text: Ability to be always in the right gear

definitions.text: Ability to be always in the right gear

parts.words: Ability to be always in the right gear
parts.note: reads like skill at driving with correct gear changes, but means a knack for wearing the right clothes

explanation.surface: Praise for a driver who never misses a gear change.
explanation.definitionFit: Having good taste in clothes means always choosing suitable outfits, gear being slang for clothing.
